title: How to Choose a Sock Manufacturer in China
description: A practical sourcing checklist for brands and buyers evaluating a sock factory in China: capability, sampling, quality control, communication and delivery.
intro: The right factory is not simply the one with the lowest quote. A reliable supplier should help turn your product brief into a repeatable production process, with clear decisions before bulk production starts.

sections.heading: 1. Start with product fit, not price
sections.text: Share the intended use, target customer, yarn preference, size range, packaging and expected order volume. A capable factory should ask practical follow-up questions about gauge, cushioning, compression, logo placement and colour tolerance before pricing.

sections.heading: 2. Check what is genuinely in-house
sections.text: Ask which steps are managed by the factory itself: development, knitting, finishing, inspection, packing and export coordination. Clear ownership of each step makes communication faster and reduces handoffs when a sample needs adjustment.

sections.heading: 3. Treat sampling as a decision stage
sections.text: A sample should confirm more than appearance. Review fit, hand feel, stretch recovery, logo clarity, colours, construction and wash performance. Record approved details in writing before issuing a bulk purchase order.

sections.heading: 4. Ask how quality is controlled
sections.text: Request a simple explanation of incoming-material checks, in-process inspection and final inspection. For performance or branded programmes, agree on the important measurements and acceptable tolerances before production begins.

sections.heading: 5. Compare total risk, not unit price alone
sections.text: A lower quote can become expensive if it creates late revisions, inconsistent sizing or avoidable rework. Compare quoted terms, communication speed, sampling discipline, quality process and the factory's ability to support repeat orders.

title: Private Label Socks: MOQ, Sampling and Lead Times
description: What buyers should prepare when starting a private-label sock programme: product brief, sampling decisions, MOQ considerations and production lead-time planning.
intro: Private label works best when the brand and factory make the key production decisions early. A clear brief reduces sampling rounds and gives both sides a realistic route to a first order and repeat production.

sections.heading: 1. Build a practical product brief
sections.text: Include style references, intended use, yarn or material preference, size range, colours, logo artwork, packaging concept and target market. If you do not have a technical pack, good photos and a reference sample are still a useful starting point.

sections.heading: 2. Understand why MOQ changes by programme
sections.text: Minimum order quantity depends on the yarn, colours, knitting complexity, logo method, packaging and whether the factory can use existing components. Ask for options rather than one number: a standard base programme may have a different MOQ from a fully custom design.

sections.heading: 3. Use sampling to lock the specification
sections.text: Approve the sample only after checking fit, colour, construction, branding and packaging. If a change is important enough to affect the customer experience, put it into the approved specification rather than relying on an informal message.

sections.heading: 4. Plan lead time from the approved sample
sections.text: Production time starts after the material, artwork, sample and commercial terms are confirmed. Allow additional time for new yarn development, complex packaging, approvals and international freight. A realistic calendar is better than a rushed first order.

sections.heading: 5. Prepare for repeatable reorders
sections.text: Keep approved sample photos, colour references, size specifications, packaging files and shipping marks in one place. This gives your next purchase order a stable starting point and makes seasonal replenishment easier.

title: Sock Materials Guide: Cotton, Bamboo and Recycled Polyester
description: A buyer-friendly comparison of common sock materials, including cotton, bamboo-derived fibres and recycled polyester, to help define a custom sock programme.
intro: Material selection changes how a sock feels, performs, costs and is communicated to the end customer. Most commercial programmes use blends rather than a single fibre, so the best choice starts with the use case.

sections.heading: Cotton: familiar and versatile
sections.text: Cotton is widely used for everyday, lifestyle and dress socks because it offers a familiar hand feel and broad consumer acceptance. Blending can help manage fit, durability and recovery, depending on the construction and intended wear.

sections.heading: Bamboo-derived fibres: soft everyday comfort
sections.text: Bamboo-derived regenerated cellulosic fibres are often chosen for a soft feel in lifestyle programmes. Buyers should define the desired hand feel and performance requirements with the factory, rather than relying on a material name alone.

sections.heading: Recycled polyester: a performance and sustainability option
sections.text: Recycled polyester can suit sports and performance socks where moisture management and durability matter. If sustainability claims will be used in marketing, discuss traceability, documentation and the exact fibre content before launch.

sections.heading: Why blends are usually the commercial answer
sections.text: Small proportions of stretch and reinforcing fibres can materially affect fit, recovery and wear life. The ideal blend depends on the target activity, knitting gauge, cushioning zones and the customer's expected price point.

sections.heading: How to choose with confidence
sections.text: Give the factory the target use and desired retail position, then compare sample options side by side. A short wear test is often more useful than choosing a blend from a specification sheet alone.
